Seminar Title:

Integrated Analytical-Computational Framework for Multiscale Fracture Insights in Concrete

Seminar Type:

Defence Seminar

Department:

Civil Engineering

Speaker Name:

Mansi ( Rollno : 521ce1012)

Speaker Type:

Student

Venue:

Seminar Room, Civil Engineering Department

Date and Time:

13 Nov 2026 09.00 AM

Contact:

Sonali Bhowmik

Abstract:

Concrete is an inherently heterogeneous, quasi-brittle material that exhibits post-peak softening under load. Its nonlinear fracture behavior is governed by the Fracture Process Zone (FPZ), an inelastic zone of damage localization ahead of the crack tip whose size cannot be neglected. This thesis develops an integrated analytical-computational framework to study concrete fracture across laboratory, meso- and atomic scales. A Digital Image Correlation (DIC)-based &ldquoboundary layer&rdquo methodology is proposed to estimate the FPZ width. It complements existing length methodologies to determine the overall FPZ size. Existing width methods show large deviations and opposing trends, whereas the proposed approach captures microcracking more accurately. Its assumption is verified through determination gradient analysis. An analytical FPZ width formulation based on the Boundary Effect Model agrees well with the DIC results, establishing the influence of the FPZ on effective strength and structural behavior. Reinforced concrete (RC) degrades under combined fatigue and corrosion. To capture this, an existing fatigue crack growth model incorporating reinforcement is modified to account for corrosion through the mass loss rate. Calibrated using Bayesian inference, the model gives reliable predictions across multiple independent datasets without re-calibration. Fatigue testing of corroded RC is time-consuming, which causes data scarcity. To address this, a &beta-Variational Autoencoder (&beta-VAE) is used for data augmentation. Three Machine Learning models trained on the original and augmented datasets all show improved accuracy with more data. A Physics-Informed Machine Learning (PIML) model embeds the analytical model in the loss function of an Artificial Neural Network. It further improves accuracy with minimal sensitivity to dataset size, offering potential for structural health monitoring. Concrete exhibits a pronounced size effect. First-order finite similitude theory is therefore applied to define the stress intensity factor of notched beams under three-point bending, and the result is validated through finite element analysis. A mesoscale analysis is also performed to capture the effect of heterogeneities on fracture behavior. At the nanoscale, Molecular Dynamics (MD) simulations model the Interfacial Transition Zone, the weakest region in concrete, as a Calcium Silicate Hydrate (C-S-H)/silica interface under uniaxial tension. Reduced chain bridging in larger models explains the decrease in strength with increasing size. Parametric studies on notch location, notch length and strain rate show that MD simulations reproduce macroscopic trends observed in experiments, reinforcing the reliability of atomistic studies. Overall, this work links full-scale, laboratory and atomic-scale investigations. It provides significant insight into the fundamental physics of concrete failure and a foundation for robust and versatile fracture characterization.
